{
  "schema": "threatline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-06",
  "sketch": {
    "components": ["Microservices", "JWT issuer logic (per service)", "JWT verification logic (per service)", "Service environment configuration"],
    "dataStores": [],
    "externalServices": [],
    "trustBoundaries": ["Service-to-service API calls", "Service process / environment variables"],
    "dataClasses": ["credentials", "secrets"],
    "exposure": "internal",
    "llmFeatures": false
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "Any service holding the shared secret can mint tokens impersonating any other service",
      "scenario": "Because every microservice holds the same HS256 secret, each service can both verify and create tokens. An attacker who compromises the least-protected service (or an insider with access to it) signs a token claiming to be the payments or admin service and calls privileged internal APIs. Symmetric signing gives no way to tell a legitimate issuer from a forger. Asymmetric signing (RS256/ES256) with per-service private keys would prevent this.",
      "component": "JWT issuer/verification logic (per service)",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Microservices authenticate each other with JWTs signed using a shared HS256 secret that is stored in each service’s environment variables." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V9.1.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-321", "CWE-290"],
      "plainLanguage": "Every service knows the same password, so any one of them can pretend to be any other.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Use asymmetric signing with per-service keys for service-to-service JWTs",
        "given": "a service needs to authenticate to another service",
        "when": "it presents a JWT",
        "then": "the token is signed with that service's own private key (RS256/ES256 or equivalent) and verifiers only hold public keys, so no verifier can forge another service's token"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "ElevationOfPrivilege",
      "title": "One leaked environment variable compromises authentication for the whole fleet",
      "scenario": "The single HS256 secret sits in every service's environment variables, so it is exposed in container specs, CI/CD pipelines, crash dumps, debug endpoints and process listings across the entire estate. An attacker who reads it anywhere - or a developer with access to any deployment config - can forge tokens for all services. Rotation requires a coordinated redeploy of every service, so in practice the secret is long-lived.",
      "component": "Service environment configuration",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "signed using a shared HS256 secret that is stored in each service’s environment variables" }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-522", "CWE-798"],
      "plainLanguage": "The same secret is copied everywhere, so leaking it once breaks authentication for every service.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Store signing keys in a managed secret store with rotation",
        "given": "a service needs its signing or verification key",
        "when": "the service starts or the key is rotated",
        "then": "the key is fetched at runtime from a secrets manager/KMS with per-service access control and supports rotation without redeploying every service"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "Stolen token is usable for 7 days with no way to revoke it",
      "scenario": "A service token captured from a log, a proxy, an error report or a compromised pod stays valid for a full week. With self-contained JWTs and no revocation list, defenders cannot cut off a known-stolen token short of rotating the shared secret for all services, which the design makes hard. The attacker keeps calling internal APIs as the victim service for days after the breach is discovered.",
      "component": "JWT verification logic (per service)",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Tokens are valid for 7 days." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-613"],
      "plainLanguage": "A stolen service token keeps working for a week and nobody can switch it off.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Short-lived service tokens with a revocation path",
        "given": "a service-to-service token is issued",
        "when": "more than a few minutes have passed, or the token is reported compromised",
        "then": "the token is rejected - lifetime is minutes not days, and a key/token revocation mechanism invalidates it immediately"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "ElevationOfPrivilege",
      "title": "Tokens can be replayed at a different service than they were meant for",
      "scenario": "The design states only that services authenticate each other with signed JWTs; it defines no audience, issuer or scope claims to check. A low-privilege service that legitimately receives a token from service A can replay that same token to a high-value service, which accepts it because the signature validates. This turns any token-receiving endpoint into a confused deputy.",
      "component": "JWT verification logic (per service)",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Microservices authenticate each other with JWTs signed using a shared HS256 secret" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V9.2.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-294", "CWE-863"],
      "plainLanguage": "A token meant for one service also opens the door at another service.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Validate audience, issuer and scope on every service token",
        "given": "a service receives a JWT",
        "when": "it validates the token",
        "then": "it rejects the request unless the issuer is an expected service, the audience names this service, and the scope/claims permit the specific operation"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "Attacker-controlled algorithm header could bypass signature checking",
      "scenario": "The design fixes HS256 only at signing time and says nothing about pinning the algorithm during verification. If a service passes the token's own header to its JWT library, an attacker can submit alg:none or switch to an algorithm the verifier mishandles and have forged claims accepted without knowing the secret. Verifiers must pin the expected algorithm rather than trust the token header.",
      "component": "JWT verification logic (per service)",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "JWTs signed using a shared HS256 secret" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V9.1.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-347"],
      "plainLanguage": "If a service trusts the token to say how it was signed, an attacker can say 'not signed at all'.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Pin the verification algorithm server-side",
        "given": "a JWT arrives with an alg header",
        "when": "the service verifies it",
        "then": "the service uses its own configured algorithm allowlist, ignores the token header, and rejects alg:none and any unexpected algorithm"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Repudiation",
      "title": "No way to prove which service issued a token",
      "scenario": "All services sign with one identical key, so a valid signature proves only that some member of the fleet produced the token. After an incident - an unauthorised internal transfer or data pull - there is no cryptographic evidence of which service or team actually issued the credential, and any accused service can plausibly deny it. Per-service keys with key ids make issuance attributable.",
      "component": "JWT issuer logic (per service)",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "signed using a shared HS256 secret that is stored in each service’s environment variables" }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-345"],
      "plainLanguage": "Because everyone signs with the same key, you cannot tell who issued a token after something goes wrong.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Attributable token issuance",
        "given": "a service-to-service token is issued",
        "when": "an incident is investigated",
        "then": "the token carries a key id and issuer claim tied to a unique per-service signing key, so issuance can be attributed to a single service"
      }
    }
  ]
}
